fig1_model: How a model feeding encounter works. (a) Dolphins maintain near-prey pressure for a minimum duration, pursue a feasible target and recover. Their rules do not change with bird presence. (b,c) Top and side views of one recorded encounter at 12 model-time units, with paths and captures from 6–12. This illustrates geometry, not proof of a compact bait ball.
fig2_returns: Absolute feeding returns and matched partner benefits through thirty-six gannets. (a,b) Captures per dolphin or gannet over the complete 36T encounter; dashed lines show matched single-species controls. Bird-only controls at each count are shared across H. (c,d) Changes relative to those controls: faint points show four paired school effects; bands and bars are exploratory pointwise 95% intervals for their means. Actual numeric bird-count spacing is retained.
fig3_opportunities: Herding duration changes strike opportunities and prey state. (a) Launches per dolphin; (b) eligible contacts per launch; (c) eligible contacts per dolphin; (d) live-fish r90. Counts cover 36T, including bird-free controls. Faint points show schools; lines join equal-school means except (b), which pools contacts/launches. r90 uses trapezoidal time averages over nonempty frames. School-state changes do not by themselves establish a feeding mechanism.
fig4_validation: Independent-school validation at fixed H1/G36: (a) dolphins and (b) gannets. Thin lines connect the same school’s label-averaged effects across encounter timesteps; faint points show the two nested labels, and diamonds the sixteen-school means. Bars are 97.5% marginal school-mean t intervals. The fine grid supplies the two co-primary endpoints; coarse-grid intervals are secondary. Axes show fish gained per individual over nominal 36T. This cohort is separate from the four-school discovery map and older eight-school check.
